title: Centuries: Tipping Points and Early Warning
outline:
The same forecasting problem across fourteen orders of magnitude in time, and the most contested material in the book. As a system approaches a fold bifurcation its dominant eigenvalue approaches zero, recovery from perturbation slows, and fluctuations show rising variance and rising lag-one autocorrelation. Marten Scheffer, Stephen Carpenter, Vasilis Dakos and Timothy Lenton formalized this into a generic early-warning framework. Since 2021 the field has taken a machine learning turn, with classifiers trained on hundreds of thousands of simulated bifurcations. The chapter treats the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation at length, and treats the rebuttals at equal length, because this is where the temptation to overclaim has been strongest and the corrections most instructive.

Built on Scheffer and colleagues in Nature 2009 and Dakos 2008, the standardized statistical toolbox, Bury, Bauch and Anand in PNAS 2021 trained on roughly 500,000 simulated series generated by continuation software, Dablander and Bury on preprocessing with the Lowess and Gaussian filters correctly distinguished, Boers 2021 and Ditlevsen and Ditlevsen 2023, Chen and Tung's Matters Arising correctly dated to 2024 on coverage artifacts and reversed proxy signs, Ben-Yami and colleagues on gap-filling and extrapolation, the August 2025 author correction that moved the tipping estimate by eight years after a Strang-splitting coding error, the Global Tipping Points Report, and the distinction between bifurcation-induced, noise-induced and rate-induced tipping.

Leaves open: a method calibrated on simulated bifurcations was applied to a system that may not be undergoing one.

verifiedClaims.claim: The generic early-warning framework for critical transitions was set out by Marten Scheffer and colleagues in Nature in 2009, arguing that systems approaching a catastrophic bifurcation exhibit critical slowing down, detectable as rising variance, rising lag-1 autocorrelation, increased skewness and 'flickering' in time-series data, and that these indicators are largely independent of the specific mechanism driving the system.
verifiedClaims.people: Marten Scheffer, Jordi Bascompte, William A. Brock, Victor Brovkin, Stephen R. Carpenter, Vasilis Dakos, Hermann Held, Egbert H. van Nes, Max Rietkerk, George Sugihara

verifiedClaims.claim: Vasilis Dakos and co-authors showed in 2008 that eight ancient abrupt climate shifts recorded in paleoclimate archives were each preceded by a characteristic slowing down of fluctuations, measured as increasing autocorrelation, beginning well before the transition itself.
verifiedClaims.people: Vasilis Dakos, Marten Scheffer, Egbert H. van Nes, Victor Brovkin, Vladimir Petoukhov, Hermann Held
verifiedClaims.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 105(38), 14308-14312

verifiedClaims.claim: Stephen R. Carpenter and colleagues provided the strongest experimental confirmation of early-warning signals by deliberately destabilizing the food web of a whole lake over three years through gradual addition of a top predator, while monitoring an adjacent unmanipulated lake as a reference; high-frequency monitoring detected rising variance and slowing recovery in advance of the regime shift.
verifiedClaims.people: Stephen R. Carpenter, Jonathan J. Cole, Michael L. Pace, Ryan Batt, William A. Brock, Timothy Cline, Jim Coloso, James R. Hodgson, James F. Kitchell, David A. Seekell, Laura Smith, Brian Weidel

verifiedClaims.claim: The concept of 'tipping elements' — large-scale components of the Earth system that can be switched into a qualitatively different state by small perturbations — was introduced by Timothy M. Lenton and colleagues in 2008, with an initial shortlist that included the Atlantic thermohaline circulation, the Greenland and West Antarctic ice sheets, Arctic sea ice, the Amazon rainforest and the Indian summer monsoon.
verifiedClaims.people: Timothy M. Lenton, Hermann Held, Elmar Kriegler, Jim W. Hall, Wolfgang Lucht, Stefan Rahmstorf, Hans Joachim Schellnhuber
verifiedClaims.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 105(6), 1786-1793

verifiedClaims.claim: An updated expert assessment led by David I. Armstrong McKay and Timothy M. Lenton concluded that exceeding 1.5 °C of global warming could trigger multiple climate tipping points, including the Greenland and West Antarctic ice sheets and abrupt permafrost thaw, with central threshold estimates for several elements falling inside the Paris Agreement temperature range.
verifiedClaims.people: David I. Armstrong McKay, Arie Staal, Jesse F. Abrams, Ricarda Winkelmann, Boris Sakschewski, Sina Loriani, Ingo Fetzer, Sarah E. Cornell, Johan Rockström, Timothy M. Lenton

verifiedClaims.claim: Thomas M. Bury, Chris T. Bauch and Madhur Anand, with co-authors, built a deep learning early-warning classifier trained entirely on simulated data — time series generated with the AUTO-07P bifurcation continuation software, labelled as fold, Hopf, transcritical or null — and reported that it outperformed conventional variance and autocorrelation indicators when applied to sedimentary records of Mediterranean anoxic events, thermoacoustic instability experiments, and paleoclimate transition records.
verifiedClaims.people: Thomas M. Bury, R. I. Sujith, Induja Pavithran, Marten Scheffer, Timothy M. Lenton, Madhur Anand, Chris T. Bauch
verifiedClaims.affiliation: University of Waterloo and University of Guelph (Bury); Indian Institute of Technology Madras (Sujith, Pavithran); Wageningen University (Scheffer); University of Exeter (Lenton); University of Guelph (Anand); University of Waterloo (Bauch)
verifiedClaims.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 118(39), e2106140118

verifiedClaims.claim: In an unusual act of self-critique, Thomas M. Bury co-authored a PNAS letter with Fabian Dablander showing that the performance of the deep learning early-warning classifier is highly sensitive to preprocessing: because every training example was detrended with a Gaussian filter of a particular bandwidth, the network implicitly requires the same filter at application time, and its apparent advantage over classical indicators shrinks when preprocessing choices are varied.
verifiedClaims.people: Fabian Dablander, Thomas M. Bury
verifiedClaims.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 119(37), e2207720119

verifiedClaims.claim: Chris T. Bauch and Madhur Anand replied to the preprocessing critique by conceding the point on filter consistency — recommending that the same filter be used for training, testing and application — while framing the deeper problem as the 'unknown unknowns' of deep learning, and calling for training sets covering a greater variety of bifurcation types and noise structures.
verifiedClaims.people: Chris T. Bauch, Madhur Anand
verifiedClaims.affiliation: University of Waterloo (Bauch); University of Guelph (Anand)
verifiedClaims.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 119(37), e2210407119

verifiedClaims.claim: Niklas Boers reported early-warning signals consistent with critical slowing down in eight independent AMOC indices derived from observational sea-surface temperature and salinity data across the Atlantic basin, concluding that the AMOC may be approaching a bifurcation-induced transition rather than merely weakening.
verifiedClaims.people: Niklas Boers
verifiedClaims.affiliation: Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research and Technical University of Munich

verifiedClaims.claim: Xianyao Chen and Ka-Kit Tung published a formal Matters Arising challenging the AMOC early-warning result, arguing that the eight proxies contain artificial increases in variance driven by expanding observational coverage over the twentieth century, that climate models with no genuine early-warning signal reproduce apparent warnings when sampled according to historical coverage, and that the sign of two of the subpolar proxies had been reversed in error.
verifiedClaims.people: Xianyao Chen, Ka-Kit Tung

verifiedClaims.claim: Niklas Boers published a reply in the same issue of Nature Climate Change defending the early-warning analysis against the observational-coverage and sign-convention objections raised by Xianyao Chen and Ka-Kit Tung.
verifiedClaims.people: Niklas Boers
verifiedClaims.affiliation: Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research and Technical University of Munich

verifiedClaims.claim: Peter Ditlevsen and Susanne Ditlevsen fitted a stochastic differential equation representing an approach to a saddle-node bifurcation to a subpolar-gyre sea-surface-temperature fingerprint of AMOC strength from HadISST covering 1870-2020, using both moment-based estimators and a Strang-splitting maximum likelihood estimator, and as originally published estimated a collapse around 2057 with a 95% confidence interval of 2025 to 2095.
verifiedClaims.people: Peter D. Ditlevsen, Susanne Ditlevsen
verifiedClaims.affiliation: Niels Bohr Institute, University of Copenhagen (Peter Ditlevsen); Department of Mathematical Sciences, University of Copenhagen (Susanne Ditlevsen)

verifiedClaims.claim: On 21 August 2025 Peter Ditlevsen and Susanne Ditlevsen published an Author Correction acknowledging a coding error in the Strang-splitting maximum likelihood estimator — the flow had been partially evaluated at time t_(i-1) rather than at the observation time t_i — identified by Anders Gantzhorn Kristensen; correcting it shifted the tipping time estimate by eight years, moving the reported window to 2037-2109 and requiring revision of Figures 5, 6 and 7 and Table 1.
verifiedClaims.people: Peter D. Ditlevsen, Susanne Ditlevsen, Anders Gantzhorn Kristensen
verifiedClaims.venue: Nature Communications 16, 7794 (Author Correction to Nat. Commun. 14, 4254)

verifiedClaims.claim: Maya Ben-Yami and colleagues showed that the observational datasets used for AMOC early-warning analysis have non-stationary missing-data distributions, and that gap-filling procedures can in some cases manufacture false indications of critical slowing down; after propagating dataset uncertainties and applying conservative significance tests, they nonetheless found the North Atlantic stability decline remained significant.
verifiedClaims.people: Maya Ben-Yami, Vanessa Skiba, Sebastian Bathiany, Niklas Boers

verifiedClaims.claim: Maya Ben-Yami, Andreas Morr, Sebastian Bathiany and Niklas Boers argued that even granting that an Earth system component is approaching a tipping point, the uncertainties — arising from modelling assumptions in the extrapolation, the representativeness of the chosen time series, and observational error plus preprocessing — are too large to permit a reliable estimate of when tipping will occur; they used the AMOC as their worked case.
verifiedClaims.people: Maya Ben-Yami, Andreas Morr, Sebastian Bathiany, Niklas Boers

verifiedClaims.claim: René M. van Westen, Michael Kliphuis and Henk A. Dijkstra introduced a physics-based early-warning signal — the freshwater transport by the overturning at the southern boundary of the Atlantic — which, unlike statistical critical-slowing-down indicators, is grounded in the salt-advection feedback, and reported that reanalysis products indicate the AMOC is on a tipping course.
verifiedClaims.people: René M. van Westen, Michael Kliphuis, Henk A. Dijkstra

verifiedClaims.claim: A modelling study led by Jonathan A. Baker provided a counterpoint to imminent-collapse claims, finding continued Atlantic overturning circulation even under extreme climate forcing scenarios, largely because Southern Ocean wind-driven upwelling sustains the circulation; the paper itself later received an Author Correction.
verifiedClaims.people: Jonathan A. Baker, Michael J. Bell, Laura C. Jackson, Geoffrey K. Vallis, Andrew J. Watson, Richard A. Wood

verifiedClaims.claim: Stefan Rahmstorf's review of the AMOC tipping question accepted that multiple independent early-warning analyses point in the same direction, but drew a sharply limiting conclusion: by the time such signals can provide a reasonably reliable warning of impending AMOC tipping it will be too late to prevent it, and observed changes in variability might have causes unrelated to an approaching threshold — an argument he treats as grounds for precaution rather than for confident prediction.
verifiedClaims.people: Stefan Rahmstorf

verifiedClaims.claim: Peter D. Ditlevsen and Sigfus J. Johnsen analysed Greenland ice-core records of Dansgaard-Oeschger events and concluded that these abrupt shifts show no critical slowing down before the transition, implying they were noise-induced rather than bifurcation-induced and therefore have very limited predictability — the paper is titled 'Tipping points: Early warning and wishful thinking'.
verifiedClaims.people: Peter D. Ditlevsen, Sigfus J. Johnsen

verifiedClaims.claim: Peter Ashwin, Sebastian Wieczorek, Renato Vitolo and Peter Cox established the standard taxonomy distinguishing three mechanisms of tipping in open systems: bifurcation-induced tipping, noise-induced tipping, and rate-induced tipping, in which a system fails to track a moving stable state because the forcing changes too quickly, even though no bifurcation is crossed. Only the first of the three reliably produces critical slowing down.
verifiedClaims.people: Peter Ashwin, Sebastian Wieczorek, Renato Vitolo, Peter Cox
verifiedClaims.venue: Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society A 370(1962), 1166-1184

verifiedClaims.claim: Carl Boettiger and Alan Hastings used large deviation theory to show that purely stochastic transitions between alternative stable states are not preceded by early-warning signals, so the presence or absence of critical slowing down cannot by itself establish that a system is approaching a bifurcation.
verifiedClaims.people: Carl Boettiger, Alan Hastings
verifiedClaims.venue: Proceedings of the Royal Society B 280(1766), 20131372

verifiedClaims.claim: Alan Hastings and Derin B. Wysham demonstrated that the class of systems exhibiting leading indicators of regime shifts is limited, constructing ecological models and identifying natural systems in which a regime change occurs with no forewarning at all.
verifiedClaims.people: Alan Hastings, Derin B. Wysham

verifiedClaims.claim: Niklas Boers and Martin Rypdal found critical slowing down in melt-rate and ice-core records from the central-western Greenland Ice Sheet, arguing that this sector is close to a tipping point associated with the melt-elevation feedback.
verifiedClaims.people: Niklas Boers, Martin Rypdal
verifiedClaims.affiliation: Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research and Technical University of Munich (Boers)
verifiedClaims.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 118(21), e2024192118

verifiedClaims.claim: A 2025 Nature Geoscience review led by Niklas Boers, with Timothy M. Lenton and Chris A. Boulton among the authors, synthesized the observational evidence for destabilization across Earth system tipping elements — including the AMOC, the polar ice sheets, the Amazon and permafrost systems — and assessed what critical-slowing-down indicators can and cannot establish for each.
verifiedClaims.people: Niklas Boers, Teng Liu, Sebastian Bathiany, Maya Ben-Yami, Lana L. Blaschke, Nils Bochow, Chris A. Boulton, Timothy M. Lenton, Andreas Morr, Da Nian, Martin Rypdal, Taylor Smith

verifiedClaims.claim: The Global Tipping Points Report, led by Timothy M. Lenton at the University of Exeter's Global Systems Institute with more than 160 authors from over 87 institutions across 23 countries, appeared in a first edition in 2023 and a second in 2025; the 2025 edition states that warm-water coral reefs are already crossing a tipping point at roughly 1.4 °C of warming, that the polar ice sheets may have passed thresholds committing the world to several metres of irreversible sea-level rise, and that the Amazon and the AMOC are both at risk below 2 °C.
verifiedClaims.people: Timothy M. Lenton
verifiedClaims.affiliation: Global Systems Institute, University of Exeter
verifiedClaims.venue: Global Tipping Points Report 2025, University of Exeter (second edition; first edition 2023)

corrections.claim: Dablander and Bury 2022 PNAS letter: because every training example was detrended with a Gaussian filter of a particular bandwidth, the network implicitly requires the same filter at application time.
corrections.correction: The filters are reversed. Bury et al. (2021) detrended all training data with a LOWESS filter of span 0.2; the Gaussian filter is the alternative Dablander and Bury tested, on which the classifier failed. Accurate text: "In an unusual act of self-critique, Thomas M. Bury co-authored a PNAS letter with Fabian Dablander showing that the performance of the deep learning early-warning classifier is highly sensitive to preprocessing: because every training example in Bury et al. (2021) was detrended with a LOWESS filter of span 0.2, the network implicitly requires that same filter at application time — stationary AR(1) series left undetrended, or detrended instead with a Gaussian filter of bandwidth 0.2, are misclassified as approaching a bifurcation — so its apparent advantage over classical indicators shrinks when preprocessing choices are varied." Correct citation: Fabian Dablander, Thomas M. Bury, 'Deep learning for tipping points: Preprocessing matters', PNAS 119(37), e2207720119 (2022), https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2207720119

corrections.claim: Chen and Tung Matters Arising, listed as year 2023, Nature Climate Change 14(1), 40-42, arguing coverage-driven variance artifacts and a sign error in two subpolar proxies.
corrections.correction: Substance confirmed, but the citation year is wrong: the paper is formally 2024 (Nat. Clim. Chang. 14, 40–42, January 2024 issue; published online 30 November 2023). The dossier is also internally inconsistent, dating Boers's reply in the same issue as 2024. Accurate text: "Xianyao Chen and Ka-Kit Tung, 'Evidence lacking for a pending collapse of the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation', Nature Climate Change 14(1), 40–42 (2024; published online 30 November 2023), https://doi.org/10.1038/s41558-023-01877-0. They argue that all eight proxies show artificial rises in variance as observational coverage expanded, that climate models with no genuine early-warning signal yield apparent warnings when sampled according to historical coverage, and that the signs of Boers's salinity proxy and one further subpolar AMOC proxy were reversed in error."

corrections.claim: Hastings and Wysham 2010 demonstrated the class of systems exhibiting leading indicators is limited, 'constructing ecological models and identifying natural systems in which a regime change occurs with no forewarning at all'.
corrections.correction: Overstates the paper: it identifies a class of MODELS, and only infers that a corresponding class of natural systems is LIKELY to exist. No natural system is identified. Accurate text: "Alan Hastings and Derin B. Wysham demonstrated that the class of ecological systems that will exhibit leading indicators of regime shifts is limited, constructing a set of ecological models — those whose nonlinearities combined with environmental variability yield descriptions without smooth potentials — for which there is no forewarning of a regime change, and arguing that there is therefore also likely to be a class of natural systems for which no forewarning exists." Citation: Alan Hastings, Derin B. Wysham, 'Regime shifts in ecological systems can occur with no warning', Ecology Letters 13(4), 464–472 (2010), https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1461-0248.2010.01439.x

corrections.claim: A 2025 Nature Geoscience review led by Niklas Boers synthesized observational evidence for destabilization across Earth system tipping elements 'including the AMOC, the polar ice sheets, the Amazon and permafrost systems'.
corrections.correction: The elements are wrong. The review assesses four tipping elements: the Greenland Ice Sheet, the AMOC, the Amazon rainforest and the South American monsoon system. It does not cover permafrost, and the ice-sheet analysis is Greenland specifically, not 'the polar ice sheets'. Accurate text: "A 2025 Nature Geoscience review led by Niklas Boers, with Timothy M. Lenton and Chris A. Boulton among the authors, presented observation-based evidence that four Earth system tipping elements — the Greenland Ice Sheet, the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation, the Amazon rainforest and the South American monsoon system — have lost stability in recent decades, and assessed what critical-slowing-down indicators can and cannot establish for each, including how oceanic and atmospheric coupling between elements can generate spurious signals or mask genuine destabilization." Citation: Niklas Boers, Teng Liu, Sebastian Bathiany, Maya Ben-Yami, Lana L. Blaschke, Nils Bochow, Chris A. Boulton, Timothy M. Lenton, Andreas Morr, Da Nian, Martin Rypdal, Taylor Smith, 'Destabilization of Earth system tipping elements', Nature Geoscience 18(10), 949–960 (2025), https://doi.org/10.1038/s41561-025-01787-0

corrections.claim: The Global Tipping Points Report, led by Timothy M. Lenton, 'with more than 160 authors from over 87 institutions across 23 countries', 2023 first edition and 2025 second edition; coral reefs crossing a tipping point at roughly 1.4 °C, ice sheets possibly past thresholds, Amazon and AMOC at risk below 2 °C.
corrections.correction: All substantive findings check out, but the participation figures are inflated by 'more than'/'over'. The report's own figure is exactly 160 authors from 87 institutions in 23 countries. Accurate text: "The Global Tipping Points Report, led by Timothy M. Lenton at the University of Exeter's Global Systems Institute with 160 authors from 87 institutions across 23 countries, appeared in a first edition in 2023 and a second in 2025; the 2025 edition states that warm-water coral reefs are already crossing a tipping point at roughly 1.4 °C of warming, that parts of the polar ice sheets may have passed thresholds that would eventually commit the world to several metres of irreversible sea-level rise, and that the Amazon and the AMOC are both at risk below 2 °C." URL https://global-tipping-points.org/ resolves and is correct for the report series; for a stable citable record prefer the report's Zenodo deposits (e.g. https://zenodo.org/records/18611781 for Section 2, Earth System Tipping Points).
